questions.q: Recording from first-hand observation means
o: drawing or photographing real objects in front of you
copying images from the internet
writing an essay
tracing a photograph
questions.why: First-hand work is valued over second-hand sources.

questions.q: Annotation in a sketchbook should
o: explain your thinking, choices and next steps
describe the weather
list materials only
be avoided
questions.why: It shows your reflection and intentions.

questions.q: Which is first-hand (primary) recording?
o: Drawing a plant you are looking at
Copying a photo from the internet
Tracing a magazine picture
Printing an artist's work
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many portfolios had little recording from primary sources, and second-hand sources were often not credited.

questions.q: Which sketchbook annotation shows the most critical, reflective recording?
o: Drawn from life over three sittings; the raking side light exaggerated the creases, which suggests ageing as a theme, and I want to test this next in drypoint.
This is a drawing of my grandmother's hands.
I like this drawing a lot.
Medium: charcoal. Size: A3.
questions.why: It records how the observation was made, reflects on what it revealed and points to a next step. The others only label or give a bare opinion.

questions.q: Why might a student record the same subject in several ways, such as drawing, photography, rubbings and written notes?
o: Because each method earns a separate mark
To avoid deciding on a direction
To gather different kinds of visual information that can support different later directions
Because drawing alone is not accepted
questions.why: Each method captures something different, such as form, light or surface, giving a richer bank of material for developing ideas.

topics.name: Explore and select materials and techniques (AO2)

questions.q: Exploring media means
o: experimenting with different materials and techniques
using only pencil
finishing the final piece first
copying an artist exactly
questions.why: Experiments show how ideas develop.

questions.q: Studying another artist's work helps you
o: understand techniques and ideas to develop your own
copy their final piece
avoid making choices
skip research
questions.why: Contextual study informs your own direction.

questions.q: Why try several media before choosing one?
o: To fill more pages
To find which best expresses your idea and develop it further
Because the syllabus bans one medium
To copy an artist exactly
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates often didn't use what they discovered to move the work forward.

questions.q: A student wants to suggest the fragility of memory in a portrait. Which choice of media shows the most purposeful selection?
o: Using whatever paint is left over in the studio
Using bright acrylics because they dry quickly
Using only an HB pencil because it is the safest choice
Layering semi-transparent tissue, faded photo transfers and partly erased graphite, after testing each
questions.why: The media are chosen and tested because their qualities (transparency, fading, erasure) express the idea. The other choices are made for convenience, not meaning.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of oil paint over acrylic paint when blending?
o: It dries much faster
It stays workable for longer, so colours can be blended wet-into-wet
It can be thinned with water
It can never crack
questions.why: Oil paint dries slowly, which allows long blending and soft transitions. Acrylic dries fast and is water-based; oil can crack if layers are applied badly.

questions.q: Developing ideas means
o: refining compositions and solutions through a series of studies
starting a new topic each week
making one drawing
choosing at random
questions.why: Show how each step leads to the next.

questions.q: How should an artist you research be used?
o: Write their biography
Analyse how their work is made and use what you learn in your own ideas
Copy one painting as your final piece
Paste in their photo
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some gave a biography instead of researching the artwork.

questions.q: What makes annotation useful?
o: It analyses decisions and explains how the work will develop
It describes what is on the page
It lists materials only
It repeats the title
questions.why: Examiners (2023): annotations were mostly descriptive rather than analytical.

questions.q: A student's line of development reaches a dead end. What is the best response?
o: Start a completely unrelated project
Remove the unsuccessful studies from the portfolio
Record why it is not working, return to earlier strong ideas and test a new direction
Make the final piece anyway
questions.why: Reflecting on unsuccessful work and redirecting it is evidence of genuine investigation. Hiding it removes evidence of the decision-making that development rewards.

questions.q: Why might a student use photo-editing software during development?
o: To try quick variations in crop, colour and composition before committing to a slower medium
Because digital work is required for this objective
To replace all drawing in the portfolio
To copy a famous image exactly
questions.why: Digital tools are a fast way to test alternatives and refine compositions. They support development rather than replace other recording or investigation.

questions.q: A final outcome should
o: realise your intentions and connect to your preparatory work
be unrelated to your research
be as large as possible
copy a famous work
questions.why: The journey to it is assessed too.

questions.q: What should a final piece show?
o: A new idea unrelated to the studies
A copy of an artist's work
Only technical skill
A personal response that grows clearly out of the supporting studies
questions.why: The journey from studies to outcome is assessed.

questions.q: How should a 3D piece be submitted in a portfolio?
o: Posted as the object
As a written description only
It cannot be submitted
As photographs
questions.why: Examiners (2023): photograph 3D objects and organic matter rather than sending them.

questions.q: Which best describes a 'personal' response at this level?
o: It is about the student's own family
It reflects the student's own ideas and decisions, informed by other artists but not imitating them
It is made without any research
It uses the student's favourite colour
questions.why: 'Personal' means independent thinking and choices, not autobiographical subject matter. Research should inform the work, not be imitated or avoided.

questions.q: How should work be selected and arranged in the submitted portfolio?
o: Include every scrap in random order
Show only the final piece
Arrange it by size from largest to smallest
Select work that shows the key decisions, ordered so the development is clear
questions.why: Careful selection and sequencing let the examiner follow the journey from recording to outcome, which is part of presenting a coherent response.

questions.q: Complementary colours
o: sit opposite each other on the colour wheel
are next to each other
are shades of grey
are only primary colours
questions.why: e.g. red and green.

questions.q: Negative space is
o: the space around and between objects
a dark colour
a mistake
the background colour only
questions.why: Using it strengthens composition.

questions.q: Linear perspective uses
o: a horizon line and vanishing points
only colour
random lines
flat shapes
questions.why: To create the illusion of depth.

questions.q: Chiaroscuro refers to
o: painting onto wet plaster
building an image from small dots of colour
strong contrasts of light and dark used to model form and create drama
applying gold leaf to a surface
questions.why: Chiaroscuro (Italian for light-dark) is strong tonal contrast, used by artists such as Caravaggio. Painting on wet plaster is fresco and dots of colour is pointillism.

questions.q: Which statement about the Impressionists is accurate?
o: They painted mainly mythological scenes in a smooth, highly finished style
They often painted outdoors, using broken brushstrokes to capture changing light
They rejected colour in favour of monochrome
They worked mostly in New York in the mid-20th century
questions.why: Impressionists such as Monet painted en plein air with visible, broken brushwork to record fleeting light. Smooth mythological painting was the academic style they reacted against.

questions.q: The A Level personal investigation combines
o: practical work with a related written analysis
only a written essay
only an exam piece
group work
questions.why: Practical and written parts connect.

questions.q: In the written personal investigation, what makes the writing strong?
o: A long biography
Copied text with no references
Only describing your feelings
Critical analysis of sources linked to your own practical work
questions.why: Cite sources and connect them to your decisions.

questions.q: How should sources be acknowledged in the written investigation?
o: Every image and quotation is credited in a bibliography or caption
Only the main artist
Not at all
Only if copied exactly
questions.why: Examiners (2023): the origins of visual work were often unclear because sources weren't cited.

questions.q: Which is the best focus for a personal investigation?
o: Art
Everything about Picasso
A focused question, such as how artists have used urban decay to explore memory, linked to the student's own practice
My favourite paintings
questions.why: A focused, open question gives the practical and written work a clear direction. Broad topics or lists of favourites lead to description rather than investigation.

questions.q: Which sentence from a written investigation shows critical analysis rather than description?
o: The painting is two metres wide and shows a woman at a window.
The artist was born in 1950 and later moved to Paris.
I really like this painting.
By cropping the figure at the edge of the canvas, the artist makes the viewer feel like an intruder, an idea I then tested in my own photographs.
questions.why: It explains how a formal decision creates meaning and connects it to the student's own practice. The others are description, biography or unexplained opinion.
